title: Mikhail Bulgakov
wiki_lead:
Mikhail Afanasyevich Bulgakov ( buul-GAH-kof; Russian: Михаи́л Афана́сьевич Булга́ков, IPA: [mʲɪxɐˈil ɐfɐˈnasʲjɪvʲɪdʑ bʊlˈɡakəf] 15 May [O.S. 3 May] 1891 – 10 March 1940) was a Russian and Soviet novelist and playwright. His novel The Master and Margarita, published posthumously, has been called one of the masterpieces of the 20th century. He also wrote the novel The White Guard and the plays Ivan Vasilievich, Flight (also called The Run), and The Days of the Turbins.
Some of his works (Flight, all his works between 1922 and 1926, and others) were banned by the Soviet government, and personally by Joseph Stalin, after it was decided by them that they "glorified emigration and White generals". On the other hand, Stalin loved The Days of the Turbins. The Soviet leader reportedly attended the play at least 15 times, even calling a theater to personally demand its production after the playwright's fall from favor. Despite Stalin's intercession in this and other matters Bulgakov was only briefly successful during his lifetime. After his death, especially once the publication of The Master and Margarita had been accomplished in 1966–67, his work was reassessed. He is now widely regarded as one of the great Russian authors of the 20th century.

Life and work


Early life

Mikhail Afanasyevich Bulgakov was born into a Russian family on 15 May [O.S. 3 May] 1891 at 28 Vozdvishenskaya Street in Kiev in the Russian Empire and baptized on 18 May [O.S. 6 May]. He was the oldest of seven children. His father, Afanasiy Bulgakov (1859–1907), was a state councilor, a professor at the Kiev Theological Academy, as well as a prominent Russian Orthodox essayist, thinker and translator of religious texts. His mother, Varvara Mikhailovna Bulgakova (née Pokrovskaya; 1869–1922), was a former teacher at a women's gymnasium. Bulgakov's godmother was his paternal grandmother, Olympiada, and his godfather was academician Nikolai Petrov.
Afanasiy was born in Oryol, the oldest son of Ivan Avraamovich Bulgakov, a priest, and his wife, Olympiada Ferapontovna. He first studied in a seminary in Oryol, and then studied in Kiev Theological Academy from 1881 to 1885, and was named a docent of the academy in 1886. Varvara was born in Karachev; her father, Mikhail Pokrovsky, was a protoiereus. Afanasiy and Varvara married in 1890. Their other children were Vera (born 1892), Nadezhda (born 1893), Varvara (born 1895), Nikolai (born 1898), Ivan (born 1900), and Yelena (born 1902).
All the children received a good education; they read the classics of Russian and European literature, studied music, and went to concerts. Bulgakov played piano, sang baritone, and enjoyed opera. In particular, he enjoyed Faust by Gounod; according to Nadezhda, he attended showings of Faust at least 40 times. At home, Bulgakov and his siblings acted out plays which they enjoyed. The family also had a dacha in Bucha.
Bulgakov was enrolled in the Second Kiev Gymasium in 1900. The next year, he was enrolled in the First Kiev Gymnasium, where he developed an interest in Russian and European literature (his favourite authors at the time being Gogol, Pushkin, Dostoyevsky, Saltykov-Shchedrin, and Dickens), theatre and opera. The teachers of the gymnasium exerted a great influence on the formation of his literary taste.
Afanasiy fell ill with malignant nephrosclerosis in 1906 and died of the illness the next year. His death caused Bulgakov to turn away from the Orthodox faith. Nadezhda observed that Bulgakov showed a great interest in the theories of Darwin and had turned to "non-belief".
In the summer of 1908, Bulgakov met Tatyana Lappa. Lappa, who lived in Saratov, had arrived in Kiev to visit her relatives; Lappa's aunt was a friend of his mother and thus introduced her to the young Bulgakov. The next year, he began to study medicine at the Kiev University. In 1912, Lappa arrived in Kiev to study. The two married in April 1913.

grok_lead: Mikhail Afanasyevich Bulgakov (15 May 1891 â 10 March 1940) was a Soviet Russian novelist, playwright, and physician whose satirical works critiqued the absurdities of Soviet bureaucracy and society. Born in Kiev to a family of Russian Orthodox scholars, Bulgakov initially trained as a doctor and served as a physician in rural Ukraine and during the Russian Civil War, experiences that informed his early semi-autobiographical writings such as Notes of a Young Doctor. After moving to Moscow in 1921, he shifted to literature and theater, producing plays like The Days of the Turbins, adapted from his novel The White Guard, which depicted the turmoil of the Civil War but drew official ire for its sympathetic portrayal of White forces. Bulgakov's career was marked by relentless censorship; by 1929, Stalin 's regime had banned most of his works, including the novella Heart of a Dog, which lampooned Bolshevik attempts at social engineering through a scientist's experiment turning a stray dog into a proletarian bureaucrat. Despite personal pleas to Stalin â who reportedly phoned Bulgakov and permitted limited theater workâhis output remained suppressed, forcing him to destroy manuscripts and endure poverty and illness from nephrosclerosis. His masterpiece, The Master and Margarita, a fantastical satire blending the Devil's visit to Moscow with Pontius Pilate's biblical tale, circulated in samizdat and was only published in uncensored form decades after his death, cementing his posthumous reputation as a defiant voice against totalitarian conformity.
